title: Answer to Question: The Coup in Niger and the International Struggle
text:
Answer to Question

The Coup in Niger and the International Struggle

Question: On Thursday 18/2/2010, military sources in Niger announced that soldiers led by Major Adamou Harouna had carried out a military coup against the country's president, Mamadou Tandja, and announced the detention of this president and the members of the government in a place near the presidential palace in the capital, Niamey, and announced the suspension of the constitution and the dissolution of all the institutions of the state. Is this coup like its predecessors, of the local struggle that used to happen in Niger between the agents of France, which holds influence in this old French colony, or is it an international struggle? May Allah reward you with good.

Answer:

Yes, this coup has happened as you said, and the formation of the "Supreme Council for the Restoration of Democracy" was announced, and that its head is "Salou Djibo", the commander of the support unit in Niamey, which includes heavy weapons such as armoured vehicles. The statement of this council said: "The government has been dissolved, and the Supreme Council for the Restoration of Democracy informs the people that the conduct of public affairs has been entrusted to the directors-general in the ministries and the governorates." (Reuters, AFP 19/2/2010)

To understand the reality of what happened, we review the following indications:

1- The French agency AFP reported that a French official, whom it did not name, had told it earlier: "A coup attempt is under way in Niger, and Tandja is not in a good position." This agency added that this French diplomat told it: "The presidential guard took part in the coup," and he said, explaining: "We know that a part of the army opposes Tandja, who imposed himself despite the provisions of the constitution, but we thought they were a minority." And he said: "There is a history of coups in this country, but we did not think it would happen this quickly." The prime minister of Niger, Ali Badjo Gamatié, had called on Wednesday, that is, one day before the coup, for an important meeting of the council of ministers.

2- All this indicates that France did not expect this coup against its agent Mamadou Tandja to happen this quickly, and that it sensed the existence of a movement among military men but thought they were a minority, that is, not influential or not capable of a coup; and that it was negotiating with them and trying to handle the situation and prevent the coup, but it happened in spite of it. The government sensed the existence of a threat to it, and it, and France behind it, wanted to resolve the problem in order to remove the threat, but the military surprised it just as they surprised France.

3- France showed its displeasure with this coup and condemned it, as a spokesman for the French foreign ministry said: "France condemns any seizure of power by unconstitutional means, and calls for a dialogue between the coup leaders and the country's president." (The American channel Alhurra 19/2/2010) The statement of the spokesman for the French foreign ministry confirms that France is against the coup leaders and wants dialogue between them and the president in order to restore him, so it is understood from this that the coup happened against it.

4- The French agency (AFP) reported on 19/2/2010 that an American official in Washington, whom it did not name, said: "(Tandja) has no one to blame but himself for the coup taking place." This agency also reported on this date, as other news agencies reported, that the spokesman for the American State Department, Philip Crowley, had declared: "This is a difficult situation. President Tandja had been trying to extend his mandate. Obviously, that is what precipitated today's events." And he said: "We believe this underscores the need for Niger to move ahead with elections and the formation of a new government."

5- The statements of the American official whose name the French agency did not mention, and the statements of the spokesman for the American State Department, indicate that America is satisfied with the coup and holds the deposed president Tandja actually responsible for the coup, in an allusion on its part to the matter of President Tandja's extension of his own term by three years through a referendum on amending the constitution which he held last August, against which the forces of the opposition rose up at the time, so that it created a turbulent political situation in the country. Tandja had been elected twice after a coup carried out by the military led by Major Daouda Malam Wanké in 1999. The constitution does not permit him a third term, so he carried out that amendment to it. He had dissolved the constitutional court for not approving the carrying out of a constitutional amendment that would allow him to stand for a third term or extend his presidential term, and he likewise dissolved parliament, and that was on 26 May last, and after that he held parliamentary elections last November, which the opposition boycotted.

The allusion of the American statements to the incident of the extension is in order to place the actual responsibility on the president and to justify the coup. Likewise, the spokesman for the American State Department did not call for the return of the president, nor for dialogue between the coup leaders and the deposed president; rather, he called for the organisation of new elections and the formation of a new government. All this confirms that America was behind the coup.

6- It is known that Niger, which is an Islamic country the majority of whose people are Muslims, was a direct French colony, and it was given formal independence in 1960, but French influence in all its forms remained in it, and "1,500" French people still reside in it to secure France's nuclear interests, as it is the third country in the world in the production of uranium, and it is French companies that exploit the production of uranium in it. For this reason it is an object of the Americans' ambitions to control it and to remove French influence from it, like the rest of the countries of Africa, most of which are Islamic countries, rich in many natural resources; they are sources of raw materials of all kinds, and likewise sources of energy, and therefore they have been an object of struggle between the covetous Western colonialists, the Europeans and the Americans.

7- Because of the importance of Niger in terms of the production of uranium, especially as it is French companies that exploit it, it is not expected that the atmosphere will clear easily for America, nor that France will leave its colonies and abandon them just like that without resisting America. Accordingly, the coming days will carry within them a heated international struggle in this Muslim country, unlike what Niger was previously accustomed to of local struggles between the agents of France.

6 Rabi' al-Awwal 1431 AH

20/02/2010 CE
